record.paper_title: Recent Results and Open Problems on the Hydrodynamics of Disordered Asymmetric Exclusion and Zero-Range Processes
record.original_question: Consider a disordered asymmetric zero-range process on Z^d in which each site x has a random jump-rate multiplier alpha_x in [c,1], particles at x jump out at rate alpha_x r(eta(x)), and the jump kernel is asymmetric with nonzero drift. For this model, Benjamini, Ferrari, and Landim proved a hydrodynamic limit only under assumptions that exclude the phase-transition regime, so the result does not describe initial macroscopic densities above the critical density rho^*. The open question is to determine the hydrodynamic behavior when the initial density profile satisfies rho > rho^* somewhere, or equivalently to extend the high-density hydrodynamic theorem now known for the special one-dimensional totally asymmetric model with r(k)=1_{k>=1} to more general zero-range processes.

evidence.quote: Problem 1. Extend Theorem 1 to describe hydrodynamic behavior also at high density ρ > ρ∗. Or, equivalently, extend Theorem 2 to more general ZRP’s.
The shortcoming of this result is that it does not indicate what happens on the hydrodynamic scale if the process starts at density above critical, that is, u0(x) > ρ∗ for some or all x.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the disordered asymmetric zero-range process on $\mathbb{Z}^d$ defined as follows. Fix a constant $c\in(0,1]$ and an i.i.d. (or ergodic) random environment $\alpha=(\alpha_x)_{x\in\mathbb{Z}^d}$ with $\alpha_x\in[c,1]$. Fix a nondecreasing function $r:\mathbb{N}\to[0,\infty)$ with $r(0)=0$ and $r(k)>0$ for $k\geq 1$, and a probability kernel $p(\cdot)$ on $\mathbb{Z}^d$ with finite range and nonzero drift $\sum_y y\,p(y)\neq 0$. The state space is $\mathbb{N}^{\mathbb{Z}^d}$; a configuration $\eta=(\eta(x))$ evolves so that, at site $x$, one particle jumps from $x$ to $x+y$ at rate $\alpha_x\, r(\eta(x))\, p(y)$.

For each $\alpha$ and each density $\rho$ below a critical density $\rho^*=\rho^*(\alpha,r,p)$, there exists an invariant product measure with mean density $\rho$; above $\rho^*$ no such measure exists, signalling condensation.

Let $u_0:\mathbb{R}^d\to[0,\infty)$ be a measurable initial macroscopic density profile, and consider initial configurations $\eta^N$ associated to $u_0$ on the scale $N$ (i.e., the empirical measure $N^{-d}\sum_x\eta^N(x)\delta_{x/N}$ converges to $u_0(x)\,dx$).

Problem: Determine the hydrodynamic limit of the empirical density at later times $tN$ (Euler scale) when the initial profile satisfies $u_0(x)>\rho^*$ on a set of positive measure. Equivalently, identify the macroscopic PDE (a scalar conservation law with a possibly disorder-dependent flux that is constant above $\rho^*$) governing the limit, in this general setting of disordered asymmetric zero-range processes on $\mathbb{Z}^d$ with arbitrary nondecreasing rate function $r$ and asymmetric kernel $p$.
artifact.category_tag: Hydrodynamic limits of disordered zero-range processes
artifact.status_search_result: Bahadoran, Mountford, Ravishankar and Saada (Ann. Probab. 48 (2020), "Hydrodynamics in a condensation regime: the disordered asymmetric zero-range process") established a hydrodynamic limit for the disordered asymmetric ZRP including the supercritical density regime, for nearest-neighbor jumps on Z with general bounded nondecreasing rate functions r. This resolves the question in one dimension with general r (going well beyond the original TASEP-like case r(k)=1_{k>=1}), but the multi-dimensional case on Z^d and the case of unbounded r or more general kernels are not fully covered, so the problem is partially solved.

status_evidence.title: Hydrodynamics in a condensation regime: The disordered asymmetric zero-range process
status_evidence.snippet: hydrodynamic limit ... including the domain above critical density, where the flux is shown to be constant ... arbitrary but bounded nondecreasing rate function
status_evidence.claim: Establishes high-density hydrodynamic limit for 1D disordered asymmetric ZRP with general nondecreasing bounded rate function r, resolving the question in this setting.
